$comment: WHICH DECLARATION'S `nocommon` (P69, lane cs; the review of the alias fold, F2). Each unit declares `int t;` and then `int t __attribute__((nocommon));`, two tentative definitions of one object. MEASURED (lane cs probe rv cell 14, nm under -fcommon): the pair is a `.bss` DEFINITION of `t` on gcc 13.3.0, clang 18.1.3 and mingw-w64 gcc 13.2.0 -- the later declaration's `nocommon` is the definition's -- so two units each written so are two strong definitions of one name, which every one of their linkers refuses as such (the measurement of examples/c/crosscu_symbol_redefined_refused, for two definitions of one name). This compiler reads the merge SURVIVOR's mark from the LAST tentative declaration (`settleNoCommon`), so it refuses the pair too, by name, and writes no artifact. The OTHER order (`int t __attribute__((nocommon)); int t;`) is the split: a COMMON on gcc and mingw-w64 gcc, a `.bss` definition on clang (probe rv cell 15) -- decided for gcc's reading, under which two such units link (their commons fold); that unit-level answer is pinned by SymbolAlias.CommonAndNocommonStateWhatATentativeDefinitionMayBe and HirLoweringC.AnUncompletedTentativeDefinitionIsMarkedOnItsGlobal, and the program runs as examples/c/two_units_nocommon_on_the_earlier_tentative_declaration. `positioned: false`: a cross-unit redefinition is a whole-program fact with no single declaration at fault. NO `runOn`: the refusal is a cross-compile fact observable from any host.
